name: Sylvia Robinson
hook: An R&B singer two decades into her career who decided rap could be sold on a record, assembled a group to do it, and was right.
blurb: Sylvia Robinson had a hit in 1957 as half of Mickey and Sylvia, and another of her own in 1973, long before hip-hop existed. In 1979 she and her husband Joe started Sugar Hill Records and did something nobody had managed: they put rapping on a record people could buy. That is where hip-hop became an industry, and the way it happened set the terms for what followed. She did not sign an existing Bronx crew. She put a group together on the spot and called them the Sugarhill Gang. The music was played by her house band rather than a DJ, and the lyrics used phrases going round the Bronx whose inventors were not credited. 'Rapper's Delight' sold over two million copies. Chic's writers were added to the credits only after they threatened legal action over 'Good Times'. Her sense of how much money there was in it was right, and years ahead of the industry. What she built on it is also the first case of a pattern that keeps coming back: the people who invented a form are not the ones who own the record.

signatureTracks.title: Love Is Strange (as Mickey and Sylvia)
signatureTracks.whyThisOne: Twenty-three years before 'Rapper's Delight'. The person who invented the rap record was not a newcomer taking a flyer; she had already had a hit career and knew how the business worked.
